utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. I did understand that the parties would prefer first to have the cross-examination of Mr. Alic, and only after that the cross-examination of Mr. Hidic. If that is true, then, Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Alic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you that you are still bound the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Alic, you'll now be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. That is Ms. Loukas. Ms. Loukas, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, when you were giving evidence yesterday, you indicated that there was a neighbour of yours, a Mirso Brkic, who you said did not agree to wear the new Serb uniform. Do you recall that evidence, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this new Serb uniform look like?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also gave evidence that on the 9th of May -- yes, you were asked this question. Mr. Harmon was reading from your statement. "On the 9th of May 1992, it was a Saturday, the Serbs announced over the Bosanski Novi radio that all Bosniaks should turn over their weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would be helpful if I could get a page number and a line number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Page 58, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Harmon would remember asking the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Harmon said to you: "I have two questions for you, Mr. Alic. Did you personally hear that ultimatum on the radio?" And you answered that yes, you had. And then you were asked this question: "Did the ultimatum apply to Muslims only? Did it apply to Serbs? Did it apply to Croats?" And you answered: "No, it only applied to Muslims because Blagaj Japra was populated by Muslims alone." So, Mr. Alic, I take it that from that answer that the answer was not directed solely at Muslims, but that your answer is that it was because Blagaj Japra was populated by Muslims alone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied only to Muslims obviously. It didn't apply to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "obviously," Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they said so. They said that Muslims, Bosniaks, should surrender their weapons. That was what the announcement said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the actual announcement said it. It wasn't just because the -- your village was only populated by Muslims, Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only on the radio. It was Ranko Gvozden who told me that. His story was the same, that Muslims should surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying it didn't apply to everybody?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this particular radio station you're talking about, to your knowledge, are you aware to whom that particular radio station broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It broadcast to everybody, Muslims, Serbs, Croats. Everybody could listen to this radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you what geographical area, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm only asking you if you know to your knowledge this radio station that you say you heard this announcement on, to what area was it broadcast to. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be heard in Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Suhaca, Agic, Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave evidence describing an attack on a military police vehicle. And of course, that attack was something that you'd been told about by other people. That was not something that you'd seen.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't see it, but other peoples did, and they told me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these people that -- I think you indicated that Izet and Sifet told us what had been told to them, and that was that: "We wouldn't be allowed to return to our homes." Do you recall that evidence, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated in your evidence that they were not officers; they just wore military uniforms. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a normal camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated that when you were put on the train that the -- that your Serb neighbours were assisting in that process of loading you on to these trains. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody assisted us. They told us to get on the train. I don't know why we should have been assisted with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you were told, you say, to get on the train. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that they were wearing camouflage military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's, of course, all you remember about what they were wearing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They also carried weapons. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mr. Alic. But in terms of what they were wearing, that's all you recall, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not wearing anything else. They just carried rifles in their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last answer seems not entirely logical to me, so I'd like to clarify the issue. The question was whether you knew anything more about the uniforms they were wearing, apart from that they were carrying weapons. Do you know any further details about the camouflage uniforms you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were multicoloured uniforms. They were not just one colour. They were multicoloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you've got no further information about insignia or...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did have eagles on their sleeves. The eagles of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, did anyone resist getting on to that particular rail car?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody objected, nobody resisted. When we realised that we had to get going, we wanted to get going as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the situation is, Mr. Alic, that you all wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We did not want to leave. We wanted to return to our homes. We didn't want to leave. However, when we realised that there was no going back, then we just wanted to move somewhere, to survive, to go somewhere where we would continue living. Nobody wanted to go of their own will. They told us that we had to go, and then we realised that it was better for us to go anywhere than to be killed there on the spot and ill-treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be true to say, Mr. Alic, wouldn't it, that you all wanted to leave, and that you were praying to God that you should leave, and that you wanted to be allowed to go because you couldn't take it any longer, and you realised you couldn't go on living there. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's five questions in one, Ms. Loukas. Would you please take your questions one by one. And would you also not ignore that you have a professional Bench in front of you. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So, Your Honour, in what sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the sense that if you say -- well, let's just assume that you're put in a situation totally unvoluntarily --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see what you're saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then ask a witness whether a way out of such a situation which he described is clearly not what they wished to say. So you have chosen this way out voluntarily, that is a way of approaching a situation which, well, might not very much assist the Chamber in really assessing what was voluntarily and not. And that is also the reason why I asked to you split up your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's a sequence of events, and the Chamber will certainly look at the sequence as a whole and not just every single bit and piece. And to say if you have -- if you are in a situation where you cannot return to your house and, as I say, that you -- well, let's say that a choice was given whether to go by trucks or by a train, even if that choice would be voluntary, that wouldn't make the situation a voluntary one. And that's more or less what I noticed. You're taking out tiny little pieces of whether there was a still a choice either to get on the train or not. Although there were soldiers there, ordered you to get on the trains, weapons in their hands, and you would have no weapons and then you say, "So you went there voluntarily." That's at least what you suggested to the witness. And this is a -- I ask you in that respect to keep your mind that what is voluntary and what is not is, to some extent, an assessment of a situation which would not perhaps entirely be left in the hands of the witness, but should be assessed by the Chamber as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. Except for the fact that I didn't use the word "voluntary." That's your word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just check what word you used, then. I have to change from yesterday's transcript to today's. One second, please. Yes, what you said. I do agree that you didn't say voluntarily. You said: "So the situation is, Mr. Alic, that you all wanted to leave," which I appreciate that you say "wanting to leave" is not exactly the same as voluntarily leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But my purpose will become abundantly clear if you'll allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be true to say, Mr. Alic, that you all wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to leave of their own will. All of us wanted to go back home. However, at gunpoint, we had to leave. And then it became clear to us that it was better for us to leave than to be killed. If somebody told you at gunpoint, "You have to leave your village," would you leave or would you stay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, the situation is that you were praying to God that you should leave and that you should be allowed to go. That was the situation, wasn't it? Would that be true to say?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We prayed to God to survive, to save our hide. We prayed to God not to be killed there and then on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you wanted to be allowed to go. Isn't that the situation, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not want to go. Once we realised that there was no other choice, that we had to leave our homes, that we were being forcible expelled from our village, then we said, "Okay, we'll go." The doors of the carriages were open, and no more words were said. If we dared to say one word, we would be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then, it would be not true to say, would it, that, "We all wanted to leave, even I was praying to God that I should leave, that I should be allowed to go because we couldn't take it any longer." It would be not true to say that, would it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it wouldn't be true to say, "I realised we couldn't go on living there." That wouldn't be true either, would it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How was I supposed to go on living there once I was forcibly expelled, when I was forced with a rifle to leave, when the door of the carriage was open for me? Would you have stayed in my place?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, do you recall giving evidence previously before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was back on the 31st of January 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I testified between the 27th and 31st of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to a question: "Was anyone resisting getting on the rail car," you said the following: "Nobody wanted to, nobody resisted. We all wanted to leave. Even I was praying to God that I should leave, that I should be allowed to go. Because we couldn't take it any longer. I realised we couldn't go on living there." Do you recall giving that answer, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I'm telling you what I'm telling you now. It was coercion. If I told you that I was praying to God to save my skin and not be killed, I think you would do the same in my place. You would tell them, "Let me go, because I see I can't live here," because the Serbs won't let me, the Serb army won't let me. I don't want to argue with you much longer about this. But it was the Serb army that forced us to go into these trains and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Alic, this morning you've said that it wasn't true that you wanted to be allowed to go; and yet, in your previous evidence, you did say that. And you've heard me read that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's at page 13941, for the record, Friday, the 31st of January 2003 in the Brdjanin case, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas, would you please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I hope my purpose has become apparent to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The purpose is apparent. Effect is apparent as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, actually stating that you wanted to be allowed to go is an important aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We took your point. We listened. We compared the testimony. So to that extent, you reached the effect you wanted, to draw our attention to the difference in wording between the testimony given in Brdjanin and what happened now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, a document has been presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If the exhibit of the record... If Exhibit Number P84 might be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that exhibit in front of you, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's indicated there that two people are present. Nijaz Ferizovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see that. I only see my sister's signature. My sister had this document issued to her in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you look further up the document, there's a name, "Nijaz Ferizovic." Can you see that now?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the name. Nijaz Ferizovic. Authorised officer, or simply officer. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see that. Now, do you know who Nijaz Ferizovic was?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a Muslim name, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is indicated there as being the official. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That's what it says here. At Ranko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Alic. Now, the situation is, Mr. Alic, that you were aware that on the 10th or 11th of May, military police patrol was attacked by armed Muslims in the village of Blagaj Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not attacked by Muslims. It was only alleged that it was attacked by the Muslims. They orchestrated the whole thing and made it look as if it had been attacked by the Muslims. But they did it themselves, to blame the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course, you've already indicated in your evidence, Mr. Alic, that you had no personal knowledge of that particular event, and it was only what you had heard from other people.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time, Mr. Alic, that you were placed on the train, did anybody give you a reason at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Dolic said to me, "You are going to Zenica, to some Serb villages, whereas people from Zenica, from these villages will go to Blagaj Japra and the surrounding villages," including Dolic. But in my view, it was actually ethnic cleansing because things didn't happen as he had indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you previously indicated that, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand this comment by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, could you please repeat what you just said because the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would have to hear the question again. I don't remember the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After you said that: "It was actually ethnic cleansing because things didn't happen as he had previously indicated," Ms. Loukas said: "Yes, you previously indicated that, Mr. Alic." And then you added something. The interpreters couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I shouldn't be repeating this. I shouldn't have to repeat this because I already said that. Why am I supposed to say things twice?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Alic, did anyone give you a reason for why you were being held at the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No reason was given. They only cursed our Ustasha mothers, made -- ridiculed us, called us "Alija's troops" and used other derogatory terms. But no reason was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have one question, Your Honour. If I could have the witness shown Prosecution Exhibit 78, and if Prosecution Exhibit 78 could be placed on the ELMO -- or not on the ELMO but on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's now appearing on the monitor. Re-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask the witness a question once he is shown the exhibit. Mr. Alic, between Croatia -- the boundary of Croatia and the boundary of Bosanski Novi, there is a river. What is the name of that river?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Una River, U-n-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Alic, the Judges have no questions for you. That means that this concludes your giving evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and answering the questions of both parties. And I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. I would like to thank you, too. And if necessary, I can come again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Alic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, for planning purposes, could you indicate how much time the cross-examination of Mr. Hidic would approximately take?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I might be able to finish before the time when Your Honour usually has the break. That's -- I wouldn't be particularly confident about that. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know that the tapes in this courtroom in urgency situations would allow us to continue for ten minutes more than we usually do. That means, I think as a matter of fact that the maximum capacity of a tape is one hour and 45 minutes. So I leave it a bit up to you. If you see at 10.30 that you would certainly not finish within 12 or 13 minutes, then perhaps we could have a break at 10.30. If, however, you think that we could finish in 10 minutes on from 10.30, then we could give it a try to see whether we can finish, and then finish for the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing perhaps I should mention, then, for planning purposes, Your Honour, is that I do have one or two other issues to raise. So if Your Honour is thinking that we could then finish for the day at that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we would have to return anyhow to hear the other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the value -- I understand the point of Your Honour's suggestion but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes. Even for the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could finish him in ten minutes and then not return after a break..

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would ask you to keep that in mind. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We would seek admission of the exhibits that were shown to Mr. Alic. Those are Exhibits 76 through 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have not given a decision on that. I did not hear any objection when they were presented to the witness. Now since they are formally tendered -- these are the Mr. Alic documents. Madam Registrar, would you then, please, read them so that we can take a decision on admission.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P76, witness statement dated 12 March 2000. And P76.1, the B/C/S translation. P77, map of BiH with Bosanski Novi highlighted. P78, map of Bosanski Novi. P79, photo of destroyed mosque in Blagaj Japra. P80, photo of front of Japra company. P81, photo of Prijedor-Bosanski Novi Road running alongside the railroad. P82, marked photo of Mlakve stadium. P83, view of the football ground at Mlakve stadium. P84, record declaration dated 09/1992. And P84.1, the English translation. P85, certificate dated 15 December 1993. And P85.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, these documents are admitted into evidence. Madam Usher, would you then, please, escort Mr. Hidic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Hannis is en route. He is descending the steps, I'm quite sure, as we speak, and when he arrives, I and Mr. Gaynor will excuse ourselves with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, may I remind that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may be seated. Mr. Stewart, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you could wait one second until Mr. Hannis returns.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I hadn't noticed. Your Honour, since we're waiting for Mr. Hannis then, may I just make this request. I'm sorry, I should have made this before the witness came in and I forgot. I wonder if Ms. Loukas could be escorted out of Court, if she would be allowed to leave Court because there is a particular task that we wish for her to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what is needed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Something is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something is needed. First of all, Ms. Loukas has my permission to leave the Court. But then I think it's a security matter rather than anything else or...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I -- well, I didn't believe Your Honour would withhold permission. But I understand there is just that -- I think there's a security aspect of opening the door to let her out, is there? If there isn't, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a guard next to the door. So if there's any problem, Ms. Loukas, if you try to leave the courtroom. You'll not be detained in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. When I suggested that Ms. Loukas should be escorted out, I didn't mean that she was getting a red card from me, Your Honour. In fact, I'm the one that's on a yellow card at the moment anyway, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's nice to see how lawyers can fill a few minutes awaiting the arrival of Mr. Hannis who has now arrived. Ms. Loukas, if there's any problem, please ask me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please ask that Mr. Stewart turns the microphone towards him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you're requested to turn the microphone to yourself when speaking. And if you put your headphones on, then you also receive all the instructions and requests from the interpreters. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, can we just remind ourselves that the town of Bosanski Petrovac, it's about 25 kilometres from the Croatian border. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to be precise, it's between 35 and 20 kilometres in the direction of Bosanski Petrovac, Kulen Vakuf, in the valley of the Una River. I think that it's the closest to the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you offered to be precise, and then offered a range of 20 to 35 kilometres when I had suggested 25. So we're going the opposite direction from precision, Mr. Hidic. I don't need precision. Is around 25 kilometres, to the nearest point of the border, is that enough? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say exactly. I told you the range that I believe to be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's about 30 minutes by normal car, normal conditions?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred to war fears beginning in 1992 earlier in your evidence. But conflict in the border area with Croatia had been a feature of life since well back into 1991, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on the Bosnian side, there was no conflict. The conflict was taking place in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. That is, outside the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina as far as the year 1991 is concerned. And the conflict was present mostly in the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think we can agree about the second half of 1991. But, Mr. Hidic, when you say that the conflict was taking place in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, I suggest to you that Croatian forces, for example, in the course of conflict, they didn't come to the border and say to themselves, "Well, excuse me, we must not cross the border," because it's in the nature of that conflict and hostilities that that is exactly what they did from time to time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that in the area where I lived such situations occurred wherein Croatian forces would come into the territory of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'd very much like to hear an answer to the question you first put to the witness; that is, whether there were any war fears, where his answer related only to the existence of a conflict. Would you please invite the witness to answer your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991, then, were there in any way war fears in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise. At what time in 1991? Was that the year you said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said the second half of 1991. And Mr. Hidic, I'm not prepared to be more precise. That is my question. Was there at any time in the second half of 1991, were there in any way war fears in Bosanski Petrovac? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. Already in that period, there was fears. A certain number of Serb volunteers from the territory of Bosanski Petrovac was involved in war operations in the territory of Croatia. If you want me to be more precise, they were engaged in the area of Knin, in the area of Plitvice, and even in the northern part of the Sava Valley, in a part called -- around Jasenovac in any case, that area. As far as I know, a certain number of volunteers from the territory of Bosanski Petrovac were engaged in those activities, and they would return to Bosanski Petrovac. And even then, you could feel the anxiety and the psychosis and fear from those people who called themselves "Kninjas" and various other names that were current at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how would -- just pause. The word or the label "Kninjas," would you define that for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say exactly, but I believe that this place name combined with the Japanese word "ninja" produced this term, to denote volunteers who were engaged in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fears that you describe in various places, just a simple question: The -- well, I'm sorry. I'll rephrase that. You said that a certain number of Serb volunteers were engaged in, and then you mentioned the area of Knin, area of Plitvice and so on. What is the nearest point to the town of Bosanski Petrovac where you recall such activities?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I think I answered this question. It is the area of Knin, the area of Plitvice, and as far as I know those people stayed precisely in those parts of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're not quite answering my question, Mr. Hidic, unless those places are the same distance away. Which of those areas that you mentioned is the nearest to Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think that Plitvice are a bit closer than Knin. But for the most part, those volunteers went and stayed in Knin. Knin was a gathering point where preparations took place involving those people who applied themselves to join; that is, volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were Serb volunteers who were engaged in activities against Croats. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went for training. And most probably, they were involved in operations if there had been such operations. From mid-1991, these parts were under the control of the Serbian Republic of Krajina. So if there were operations, these people would be engaged in those operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, Mr. Hidic, that for all practical purposes, Muslims and, of course, Croats who were in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not participate in such preparations and such operations that took place involving Croats? Or Croat forces. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking exclusively about volunteers. There were no volunteers among the Muslim people. I've also said that a certain number of Croats, an insignificant number, maybe 48 to be very precise, resided in the territory of Bosanski Petrovac. So there were no Croat volunteers at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How precisely, Mr. Hidic, can you put the beginning of these war fears in 1991?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was talking about the year 1992, about April 1992 when one could feel these changes that emerged. In 1991, there were some occurrences that instilled fear among people in Bosanski Petrovac, those who the participated in such operations, when they returned to Bosanski Petrovac, they started using weapons. They started shooting in the evening. They wanted to make it known that they were volunteers, that they belonged to a certain armed force. I hope this answer will be to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, it isn't, as it happens, Mr. Hidic. But Mr. Hidic, I make full allowance for the fact that I have far more experience of asking questions in Court than you do of answering them. It's only fair to recognise that. But Mr. Hidic, you are not listening, with respect, carefully enough to the questions. And please, will you do that. And it's not a free-ranging discussion here, Mr. Hidic. If I ask you a question, if you don't understand it, then of course, please, say so. But if you do understand it, then please listen to it and give the answer to that question. So the question was and is, how precisely can you put the beginning of those war fears in 1991? And I will simply add, then, if it helps to clarify, I'm asking you to be as precise as possible as to the date when those fears began to appear.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in my previous answer I have already given you most of the answer. There's no precise date. If I tell you that during 1991, from the very beginning of that year, there were already checkpoints on the roads leading from and to Bosanski Petrovac, this points to the fact that a war already started in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you personally were not involved in any way in any such military activity, potential military activity, or such preparations as there might have been for any war or fighting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is correct. It is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I confirm what you have stated. I personally was not involved in any war activities. I was not militarily engaged during that period. I was not a soldier. Therefore, I did not have an opportunity to -- now you have put me in a situation that I don't know how to answer your question. I was not militarily engaged, to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, there's no problem about this. It's the perfectly natural point that sometimes a witness answers no or yes when it's necessary to clear up the ambiguity for the record. That's not a criticism of you at all, Mr. Hidic. It's just something that we sometimes need to do. And we've done it. Thank you. And it's also correct, is it, that as you said already that you were -- in 1991 and 1992 you were not even a member of the SDA. Is it correct that during 1991 and 1992, you were in fact involved in no political activity of any sort whatever?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you never attended any of the meetings, certainly not SDS meetings, but you never attended any of the meetings at all mentioned in any of the documents which you have produced in Court or provided to anybody in connection with this matter?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're talking about documents which were produced in 1992. Those documents did not originate from 1991. Those are documents by the Crisis Staff from 1992. In 1991, I still worked in Bosnaplast. I was not engaged in politics. I was only engaged in my own profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hidic. I think you are right. There probably aren't any 1991 documents. I was just being cautious. So we have that clear. Is it also correct that you were never personally aware in 1992 of any instructions by the SDS Main Board to any local board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. I found it very hard to follow it. I apologise. I really wasn't able to follow you -- the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. Hidic. I invited you to seek clarification, and I'm very happy to give you the question again. Is it correct that in 1992, you were personally never aware of any sort of instructions given by the SDS Main Board to any local board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't know anything about such documents at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was in the area of Bosanski Petrovac a rally organised. I suggest to you it was in 1990. During a burial in -- excuse me. In Krjneusa. Acknowledgments to my case manager. Krjneusa. Do you know something about that rally?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, yes. This rally was accompanying the exhumation, that is, the taking the bones from Risovack Jama, not far from Krnjeusa in the direction of Bosanska Krupa. The distance is between 10 and 20 kilometres. So this is the location we're talking about, Risovacka pit, between Krnjeusa and Bosanska Krupa. And this was a well-known event in Bosanski Petrovac when this was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree it was 1990, Mr. Hidic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what month or around what time of the year?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I believe that this was in the second half of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't personally attend that rally, did you, Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you came to hear from others about it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of comments by the Serbs who attended that rally and who were there on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct that you were told, is it, that Dr. Biljana Plavsic was there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the testimonials of the Serbs who were there, the entire Serbian leadership was there, and this included religious officials, Patriarch Pavle. And on that day, when these bones were being reburied, the complete leadership was there. I don't know what happened. All I know is that this rally did take place, and this is the extent of the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I wonder if we could have a few minutes. I wanted Ms. Cmeric to ask Mr. Krajisnik a question, but actually he has answered a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, take your time, take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, do you remember -- you had specifically mentioned Dr. Plavsic in previous evidence that you have given before in this Tribunal, in the case involving Mr. Brdjanin. Do you remember the names of any other Serb leaders that you haven't mentioned that you were told were present at that rally?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know for sure that the patriarch of the Serbian church, Pavle, was there. People talked about the way he spoke. I know that all the local officials were there. And according to the words of the people who were there, some Serb officials were also there, delivered speeches, spoke to the people. But I can't remember who they were. At that time, I worked in a cafe bar. It was at the main bus stop. People who were returning from that rally were talking about the things that had gone on in Krnjeusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Hidic, that you never heard anybody say that Mr. Krajisnik had been present at that rally?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever in your life met Mr. Krajisnik? You see him here today in Court, of course. But have you ever met him before?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Krajisnik very well from TV. However, I never -- I've never had an opportunity to meet with him and to talk to him face to face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1991 and 1992, did you see Mr. Krajisnik from time to time on television in his capacity, in the first place, as the Speaker or the president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. If you want me to be more precise, I remember Krajisnik most from the war period and the post-war period when he held certain posts at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that's when he appeared on TV quite often. That's when I saw him on TV quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Talking about 1991 and 1992 for the moment, Mr. Hidic, and casting your mind back, what did you know during those two years about Mr. Krajisnik's position in the politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina and subsequently Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have already said that I was not interested in politics. I was not interested in any of the individuals who were engaged in the politics. I just read newspapers and that it was all my engagement. To be honest, at that time, I was not interested in Krajisnik. I did not focus my attention on him. I never gave Krajisnik a second thought. And I did not seek any particular information about him. I knew about him as much as I could get from the media. At the moment, I would just skim through the papers or just listen to the news, and I would not make an effort to retain any of that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know, for example, that he was the -- in 1991, that he was the Speaker or the president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say. I was not aware of his position. I was aware of some other Serb officials who were members of the assembly because you could read those names on a daily basis in the newspapers. It would be -- it would not be fair for me to say anything about Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour. We're just trying to clarify something on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Ms. Cmeric suggests that - and she is nearly always right about these things - that in the answer to the previous question where the transcript shows in English: "I was aware of some other Serb officials who were members of the assembly because you could read those names on a daily basis," that the word in the witness's own language would be more aptly translated as "Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, where it reads "assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, where it reads "assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the witness again, because otherwise we'll have to re-listen to tapes. When you said, Mr. Hidic, that: "I was aware of some other Serb officials who were members of," and then -- is that the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you then say? Members of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the matter has been clarified now. I even could hear it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Hidic, then, so having clarified that, you were aware of some other Serb officials who were members of the presidency. That was the position, was it, in 1991, your awareness?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if that is the answer you have been expecting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, then, can you name any of those other Serb officials who as far as you saw it at that time were members of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you one name. Nikola Koljevic. I also know Mrs. Plavsic. I believe that this will suffice. I'm aware of these two persons who were certainly members of the presidency in Bosnia and Herzegovina while the presidency still consisted of representatives of the three peoples. There were also other representatives who were the so-called neutral members of the presidency who did not necessarily represent any of the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Hidic, that you also have no knowledge whatever of Mr. Krajisnik having been involved in any of the matters to which you have previously referred in your evidence in this case or, indeed, in the Brdjanin case?.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to object to the form of the question. "Involved in," is fairly ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do, so Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- involved is very general, but it is deliberately very general because that's the fair way of offering the question to the witness because it's giving him the widest range of opportunity to say yes, he is, and then, depending on his answer -- well, I won't say any more because the witness still has to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether the witness has to answer the question also depends on the following: Mr. Hannis, does the Prosecution present the evidence of Mr. Hidic, including the documents you presented, as evidence of the events in Bosanski Petrovac and people involved locally, or does the Prosecution also draw any conclusions as far as the involvement of Mr. - and I'm now using the word to, give you the widest opportunity to respond - the involvement of Mr. Krajisnik specifically in these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess what I'm concerned about is that "involved in" in some sense perhaps involves a legal conclusion that will be reached after all the evidence is in in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Everything is related to everything. But we now see that the Defence is seeking confirmation that Mr. Hidic, who did not speak about the role of Mr. Krajisnik or any specific involvement of Mr. Krajisnik. But I wonder, these questions are only necessary, I would say, if the Prosecution would conclude from this evidence that there was any specific involvement of Mr. Krajisnik. If that's not the position of the Prosecution, we could then move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what I would like to do at this point is withdraw my objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very handsome of Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's give you the question again, Mr. Hidic. That's only fair in the circumstances. I've now lost it off the screen. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can stop the screen, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It depends which screen, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one of the screens. I'll read the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question to you, Mr. Hidic, was whether it is correct that you also have no knowledge whatever of Mr. Krajisnik having been involved in any of the matters to which you have previously referred in your evidence in this case or, indeed, in the Brdjanin case. That was the question to you. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to the local level, the Bosanski Petrovac level, I really did not have any information about any personal involvement by Mr. Krajisnik in the territory of Bosanski Petrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, when you returned to Bosanski Petrovac late in 1995, which is what you have told the Court, what -- it wasn't absolutely clear, I think, from your evidence, but what particular function or responsibility, if any, was it that led you to gather the documentation that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was engaged by the civilian body of government involved in humanitarian issues. I have access to these documents. I could enter the building of the municipality every day because I had my office there. And from that office, I conducted the business that I was hired for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that your -- was that your full-time job then at that stage?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not paid at first, so my working hours were not defined. I worked as the need arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the position that -- you were still working, then, were you, as a skilled locksmith or as a warehouse manager at that time? 1995.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a paid job at the time when you started work for this organisation you've mentioned, this body?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about 1995. In 1995, on my return to Bosanski Petrovac, nothing worked. So I could not go back to my previous job. I performed certain duties as needs arose. There were not enough natives of Bosanski Petrovac at that time. The authorities were set up, and I was appointed to be involved in humanitarian issues because that's something that I had already done on behalf of the refugee community of Central Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of the civilian body of government involved in humanitarian issues that you mentioned a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that there was no well-defined body or organisation that would deal with it, we were sort of organised, sponsored by the Red Cross and similar organisations. After the arrival of representatives of UNHCR, the leaders of the local administration charged me with coordinating these affairs in cooperation with humanitarian organisations, including international organisations in the area of our canton. That involved contact with local humanitarian organisations and international ones, primarily the UNHCR which was based in the Sana canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were specifically engaged, were you, to gather documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My task was not specific. But since I found a lot of documents simply scattered around the premises, and they were accessible to anyone who happened to enter the building, because at the time normal life had not been restored in the municipal building. Those documents were available to anyone, including me. And I told my co-workers not to throw these documents away, that it's better to keep them. And they started gradually to bring them to me. I put them in order and safeguarded them. Of course, God knows how many documents were lost or were taken away God knows where. But I repeat, those documents at the time were available to anyone who happened to come in. All the offices were open. All the cupboards were open. All the shelves were there. Things were lying on the floor. And it is very likely that during the withdrawal, somebody was looking for specific documents and scattered the rest all over the place. And certainly, there were other documents which were piled in neat stacks on the shelves in certain offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's convenient for the Tribunal, that's as convenient a point as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hidic, we'll take a break of some 25 minutes. And do I understand how much time could Mr. Hidic expect more or less to be further cross-examined by you, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Something like about 15 minutes, Your Honour, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, we'll have a break until 11.00. And then it might take another altogether half an hour, perhaps a little bit more. I'm not talking about cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be re-examination and perhaps some questions from the Bench as well. We adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for being back late. It might be of some comfort to the parties to know that it was because the Judges conferred on a matter we discussed yesterday during our meeting, so that caused the delay. I couldn't say that we have finished our internal discussions yet, but I'm quite confident that we'll come up either late this morning or early this afternoon with at least some clear messages. And even if the parties would be available to briefly meet, then, again in order to hear what the Chamber considers to do, that would be good. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis is smiling at me because he can see for the moment in the light of what I said to him a few minutes ago the position this puts me in. I had indicated to Mr. Hannis over this break just now that I would be making an oral motion to the Court in relation to this area this morning. However, I don't want to make unnecessary applications if the Bench is still conferring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm quite confident if we would finish the examination of Mr. Hidic in, let's say, approximately half an hour altogether or 40 minutes, then the Chamber would further meet. And I am confident that it will take us not more than 20 or 30 minutes to come to a conclusion, and then invite the parties to meet and hear what the conclusions of the Chamber are. I leave it up to you whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would give me -- may I just on a technical and practical level, that meeting, would that be back in open Court then, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be in open Court, I think. There's no problem with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would give you an opportunity that if we come with a message you wouldn't like, you could still make --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is reading my mind and interpreting what I've said. And there is also one other matter that we have to raise. But it would make sense, then, in light of what Your Honour has said if we leave that other matter to the very end so that Your Honours have the opportunity of conferring straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I take it that you're informed about meetings that took place, and these are rather practical scheduling matters, trying to meet the needs the Defence has expressed, and at the same time to keep -- you have no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had very little chance to speak to my Defence counsel. But I hope I will be able to get some information once they are free, because they seem to be busy all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good that they are busy, Mr. Krajisnik. Keep them busy. Perhaps when the Judges meet, if you would have an opportunity to update Mr. Krajisnik, because -- I'm not interfering in your relationship with your client. Of course not. But I'm also aware that we met yesterday late, that there was hardly any time, I take it, to discuss matters with him. But perhaps if you could use that time, that would certainly save perhaps some time later to explain to Mr. Krajisnik the course of events during our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Krajisnik does keep us busy. We keep him busy as well. And of course we have spoken to him his morning on other matters, but Your Honour is right. We simply haven't had the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully understand. Then are you ready to finish the cross-examination of Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All I need is the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher is already finding the witness in order to escort him into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, please be seated. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, are you saying -- I wasn't entirely following the answers you gave immediately before the break as to the nature or name of this civilian government body that you had mentioned. Are you saying that there wasn't a specific body or organisation that engaged you on this work?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was a body established in exile called the War Presidency of the Bosanski Petrovac Municipality. And I think, to add to my answer, I believe it was set up sometime in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the War Presidency of the Bosanski Petrovac Municipality is that civilian body that you referred to earlier that had engaged you for a number of tasks, one of which became this gathering of documents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This war body existed -- this wartime body, this presidency in exile, its main role was to gather humanitarian aid and to provide for displaced citizens from Bosanski Petrovac, for refugees. And it also served as a link with those who were outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I mean, primarily Croatia and other countries, because to this day there are citizens of Bosanski Petrovac scattered all over the world. And it was not solely focussed on war issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, you're not quite answering my question in a specific way. You referred earlier to a civilian body of government, I think, is what came over on the transcript. A civilian body of government that had engaged you on a number of tasks, and that was in the context of the work that you had done in Bosanski Petrovac in gathering documents and examining documents. I have in one way or another I think now asked you several times to give the Trial Chamber the name of that civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure - perhaps I remember incorrectly - but I don't believe that the witness has testified that gathering documents was one of the tasks for which he was employed. It was simply something that he did in connection with his presence there when he was employed on other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I accept that up to a point. And I think I recognise that it was really the clear implication of what he had said that it included the gathering of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just in case there's any doubt or difficulty about that, I can leave that on one side, and I can simply ask you, forget about documents, confining it. The civilian body of government that you referred to that was involved in humanitarian matters that engaged you on a number of tasks, what was its name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, in September of 1995 when I arrived in Bosanski Petrovac, that was still at a time when there was a war, a state of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is, September of 1995. In December of that year, the Dayton Accords were signed, and civilian governments, transition civilian authorities, were established. In those municipalities which were unfortunate enough to have governments in exile, they could return after September or December 1995. And governments were supposed to be formed based on electoral results from 1991. Since at that time Bosanski Petrovac was populated only by us, Muslims, this is the way this transitional government was formed. And it was -- if you allow me to say one more thing so that you have a clearer picture. In September 1995 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, please pause now, then. I, with the Trial Chamber's permission, will allow you to say one more thing, but that one more thing that I would like you to say is the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. First of all, tell us the one thing you'd like to say. And I might have a question of you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in September of 1995, upon arriving to Bosanski Petrovac for a four- or five-day visit, I continued to travel to Zenica where I organised the return of Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac to their municipality and that took me more than a month. I lost that time organising the return of about 900 Bosniaks who were at the time located in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you the following: When you returned, when you had your office, when you saw documents scattered around which you started gathering, by whom were you then employed, paid or unpaid? Was that the transitional -- as you told us, the transitional government, or by any other body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no specific task. Nobody gave me that task. I simply got hold of certain documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You had an office where you saw these documents in the same building lying around. Who gave you that office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course it was the leaders, the person who was in charge of the organisation and functioning of civilian life in the area of Bosanski Petrovac after the war, after my return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you call the transitional government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I'm not satisfied with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not -- if you have any addition questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred very --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for pursuing that. When I say I'm not satisfied, Your Honour understands what I mean, I hope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to a civilian body. I'm just going to read it. The precise phrase was, "Civilian body of government involved in humanitarian issues." And this was some time ago. That body, that was in your own language, that was your word, did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it was not a body. And that body of civilian government, I was in charge of humanitarian issues, humanitarian affairs. Since I had already dealt with such affairs in exile, I helped accommodate and provide for displaced persons from Bosanski Petrovac. That is why in that transitional municipal authority I was given the same task. I was charged with the same duties until the government started to operate fully. Because it was not already by that time decided yet whether we belonged to the Una Sana canton or some other canton. Our municipality had at that time not been clearly defined yet as a unit of the Una Sana canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were asked at the time, or if you had been asked at the time when engaged in this humanitarian work, Mr. Hidic, who do you work for, what would you have said?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski Petrovac, I would have said. And that's how I introduced myself to people. Whenever I had to go to other towns on various business, I was a man from Bosanski Petrovac dealing with humanitarian aid. And that's how people knew me. Specifically if I had dealings with the UNHCR or the Red Cross or the headquarters of the canton in Bihac or the Merhamet charity organisation or any other organisation, I was the man from Bosanski Petrovac in charge of humanitarian aid. And if you allow me to expand, in Bosanski Petrovac at that time, we had not a single humanitarian organisation that was registered as such, fully in keeping with the legislation in the territory of the Una Sana canton. Not a single one. Only later did they arrive. And I worked together with those organisations that later arrived, humanitarian organisations, as a contact person, as a coordinator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, we sometimes see on our televisions the man from Del Monte, and everybody knows who he is. But when you were introducing yourself to the Red Cross, for example, saying you were the man from Bosanski Petrovac, now, Mr. Hidic, they would have wanted to know who you represented before they sat down and talked to you. Who did you represent when you went to meetings with the Red Cross and the other organisations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've already answered that. I represented Bosanski Petrovac, the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- have you ever had any connection with a Bosnian state organisation called -- in English the acronym is AID, A-I-D?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it do? Sorry, what did it do in 1995 or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I had no contacts with that body, and I wouldn't know what that body was engaged in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gathered up or collected from people these documents in 1995 in Bosanski Petrovac in the way that you have previously described, what was your own next task in relation to those documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any specific tasks with regard to these documents. The documents of some interest to me dated from 1992, and that is the period during which Bosniak Muslims were still in Bosanski Petrovac, up to the moment of their exile. So that is the only thing that I was interested in because the majority of the documents in the room where I worked were from that period. And that's how actually my interest became aroused, when I saw documents that concerned us, Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac and the period of time that was relevant, the year 1992. That's how I started gathering those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what topic you were interested in before you collected the documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was curious more than anything. And I wanted to compare the things that I knew were happening with the statements of Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac that appeared in various newspapers. In some way, I just expanded on my knowledge of the events that I was aware of. In other words, this just confirmed the things that I already knew that I had been through during the period between April and September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, you've talked about a Crisis Staff of which in your evidence, by and large, the members of the Crisis Staff were Serbs. That was at page 111 of the transcript of yesterday. At any point in 1991 or 1992, did the Muslim community and/or the SDA have its own Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you, in relation to appointments in 1991 and 1992, before the war, appointments to the police, that those appointments were made by order of the minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina [sic]?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which hierarchy was in place for the appointment of police officers. At that time, I believe that there was a political agreement on the candidates that would be given jobs in the police. I am aware of the person who was the candidate of the SDA. He was not a member of the SDA, but he had a degree in law. And this experience tells me that the candidate for the chief of police was a Serb and the candidate for the commander of the police was a Bosniak. This never came through in the way it had been arranged, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who, before the war, the minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina was?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I -- does it jog your memory, does it affect your answer if I suggest to you it was Alija Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in Bosanski Petrovac, things were what they were. I'm aware of the complete situation in Bosanski Petrovac. Anything beyond that just did not interest me. I was at the time a member of the working class. The only thing I was interested in was work. Politics did not interest me at all. During that period of time, I was ill for a certain while. So I was really not interested in who was who in the politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Hannis, any need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. A couple of housekeeping matters when we are completed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions for you, Mr. Hidic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us in respect of one of the documents we discussed yesterday about Obrad Vrzina who you said was a military man. Would you have any further details apart from that he was a military man? Would you know which forces? What rank? Well, would you know anything more than him being a military man?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have stated that he was a military man, but he was the chief of the Territorial Defence. That was his position, something like that. So by virtue of his position, he was invited to the meetings of the Crisis Staff. I don't know whether he was its permanent member. But he did attend some of its sessions, especially those dealing with mobilisation. That's when he would attend sessions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you, answering a question of Mr. Stewart, you said that an organisation called AID, you had no contacts with them and that you didn't know what they were engaged in. Did you know about the existence of such an organisation, even when you had no contacts and even if you wouldn't know what they were engaged in? Does the name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, and I read in the newspapers and I learned from the media that there was this AID. I myself did not have any points of contact with this organisation. I did not cooperate with this organisation. The AID was and has always been a body that was a point of interest in the media, just like any other institution of that sort. The AID is still mentioned in the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got no idea of the relevance of that question. But could you tell us what the press says the AID is? Because I've got no idea.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
