utterances.text: I believe that it was a service that was established within the Muslim/Bosniak Corps as far as I know. I really wouldn't be able to tell you more about this service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then finally about the documents, the bundle of documents you gathered. In your statement you say that you couldn't specifically say which document came from where. Would that still be true? Do you know from certain documents which ones they -- where they come from, even perhaps not knowing from all of them where they came from? Could you give us a bit more detail? Could you tell us, for example, 90 per cent came from the building in which I had my office, or 50 per cent, or only those working in the building gave me those documents? Well, I'd like to have some more details.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the documents came from the offices of the president of the Executive Board, secretary of the Executive Board of Bosanski Petrovac Municipality during the times of war. The war president of the Executive Board of Bosanski Petrovac Municipality and his secretary. Some of the documents also originate from the office of the president of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say they originate from the certain sources, do you mean to say by that that they are related to those institutions, or that you got them from a person related to that institution? Do you understand what my question is? My question is it could be the cleaner of the building that would given the document to you, although it relates to the office of the president of the municipality. I'm making a clear distinction by from whom you got them and what organisation might have created the document.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the documents were found in the aforementioned offices. Somebody found them. They were either sitting on the desk or at the places where one could see what kind of documents those were. That's how some of these documents that I took an interest in when I saw them, because they specifically described the period that was relevant to me, and that is the period between April and September 1992. I was not interested in any other documents that went beyond that period. And that's how I gathered those documents. There were documents covering other periods of time while these bodies were operational, the year 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are quite a lot of minutes of the sessions of the Crisis Staff of Petrovac among the documents. Do you remember how you got those minutes? Were they in binders or were they also scattered on the floor? Because I see that we have some subsequent series, the 24th Session, the 25th Session, the 26th Session, the 27th Session. Do you have any recollection on how you got those documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were stored somewhere, but later on they were scattered around. And that's how I found them. And they were not the only copies. There were several copies of those documents which were either in folders or binders or were scattered in the room or in other places where I could get hold of them. Some of these documents were in the office of the president of the municipality. Some were in other -- in the other room or at other places where the former members of this body had left them and stored them as documents that they would need or that they had used during meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your personal markings on these documents, and Mr. Hannis, I draw your attention to the fact that on some of the documents the handwriting markings are translated and others are not. That is not a very consistent way of presenting this evidence. Would that give you any information on where you got them from, or would that not assist you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this just marks documents which were scattered, which were not in any particular order. For example, I would have number 35, and then number 45 would be found somewhere else. And that's how I marked those documents, in order to prevent other people from getting hold of them. And that's what inspired me to gather other such documents which were in a certain sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be given the set of documents. That's -- Madam Registrar, P90 it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a comment at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding the documents, in his prior testimony in Brdjanin and also in his prior ICTY statements, there is some detailed discussion about individual documents and where he found the documents, et cetera, that may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But there's also now and then an answer that he doesn't know exactly on all documents. So could I take you to document 21. Mr. Hannis, 21, for example, doesn't give any translation of the handwriting on the right top corner of the document. Could you take the original, the B/C/S original in front of you, and perhaps read the number on the right top corner stamped on it so that we know for certain that we have the same document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11/1992, registered as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to stop. Do you see stamped as a number on the right top corner 02930159?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then perhaps read your handwritten part on top of that. You just started doing that. Could you please finish that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11/92 [Realtime transcript read in error "11/1992"], registered as evidence, or recorded as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this give any clue to you in respect of where you found it or from whom you got it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was found in a manner that I explained. As for its registration, we had a protocol that was in the office. Unfortunately, the book has gone missing. And that was my motive for some of these documents to be preserved, not to go astray, because these documents were accessible to practically anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this document has been found in the building where you had your office?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take you to Document 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for complete accuracy, Ms. Cmeric points out that the transcript records that the marking is 11/1992. Just for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 92, and that's -- of course, we can read that as well. That's not -- it's not of vital importance to my question. The most important is that the ERN number that we compared --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. But it is, nevertheless, as we suggest, it's important that as far as possible the transcript does get these things absolutely a hundred per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Stewart, for assisting me. Could I then take you to Document 31, which is a letter. And under the signature, we see that the signature is -- should at least be from Mr. Rajko Novakovic. Could you tell us, since there is no handwriting on this document, do you have any recollection or have you any clue from where you got that document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is from the office of the president Novakovic, whose signature is on the document. So it originates from his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that just on the basis of the signature that you conclude that it must have come from the office of the Crisis Staff president, or do you have any further recollection of how you got it, which confirms your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was in the office. And I got it - how to put it - from the president that occupied this office after the liberation of Bosanski Petrovac. This document was accessible to everybody, again. But this is how I got hold of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Thank you very much for your answers. Do the questions of the Bench raise any need to put further questions to the witness? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, you indicated in answer to His Honour's questions that you were interested - I hope I'm paraphrasing pretty accurately - you were interested in the period April to September 1992. It sounds as if you were -- you had decided or somebody had decided for you in advance of coming across these documents that that was your period of interest. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is not the motive that governed me. The reason is that during that period of time I also kept my own diary, and I just was curious to know whether I as an individual was able to record accurately the events that were happening in the territory of Bosanski Petrovac. In other words, I was just curious to see whether my description of these events was really accurate. That was my only intention. And I didn't have any other reason to collect these documents. Within the context of my writing of the diary, I continued doing that in the exile until the moment I returned home in the year 1995. I described different situations, but I was mostly interested in Bosanski Petrovac municipality because Bosanski Petrovac is the town where I was born, where I grew up, where I was born and raised. And I was interested solely in this period because I just wanted to complete the information that I had in my own head. I wanted to complete it somehow with other sources of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about information, Mr. Hidic. There's a great deal of information in the answer you've just given. Unfortunately, it doesn't include an answer to my question. The -- I asked you -- we take it that you were interested in the period April to September 1992 because you've said that, and you've said it more than once. I had asked you if, when you came across these documents in the way you described, you had already decided or somebody had already decided for you that April to September 1992 was the period you were interested in. Is that or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see where you're coming from. However, I did not have a task. This was my own personal desire, my personal intention to compare these things what -- with what I saw. Within that context, I can give you some statements that originate from the beginning of the war that illustrate the state that I was in. So there was no imperative. There was no predetermined desire. It was all my personal desire to do things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, the question clearly was whether you had in your mind when you started gathering these documents that you would limit it to this period, or was it that you decided later to limit it to that period? Was there any moment where you thought, well, let me concentrate on April until September 1992. And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that there were no documents that covered other periods. Most of the documents covered the year 1992. As for the year other periods, there was just a book of hand-recorded minutes of the meetings that took place in 1993, 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you, then, that your choice of the documents you collected was mainly determined by what you found and not by a decision taken by yourself or by anyone else that you would limit it to this period? Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I mentioned any restrictions. I was personally interested in that period, April/September 1992. That documentation, Your Honour, does not include all the documents covering all the events of that period. It means that they were not found. They were no longer in that place where they had been stored. A large number of documents for that period is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it's not a complete set. Any further questions, even if on this subject. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think this is the only subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you believed there were no documents that covered other periods. So what we got from you is there were no documents that covered any period other than April to September, but at some point, which still remains not totally clear, you were only interested in April to September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said there were hand-recorded -- these are documents as well. Hand-recorded minutes of the meetings that took place in 1993, 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are documents. And so he said one thing, but the next line, he said -- he further clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm coming to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before April 1992, do you say there were any relevant -- delete relevant. Before -- for the period before April 1992, do you say there were any documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I understand what Defence counsel is driving at. Yes, of course. In the second half of 1992, the so-called national or people's -- I can't remember the exact name now, but I believe it was the committee or board. What was the name of that body? The board for people's defence, or the committee for people's defence, which also was supposed to represent all ethnicities in different positions. Let's say it was the national committee. It functioned along the same lines as the Crisis Staff with the proviso that there were two Bosniaks on that board. One was vice-president of the municipal assembly and the other one was dealing with military issues. He was head for national defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, once again, your answer, though containing a certain amount of information, doesn't appear to be linked in any intelligible way to my question. I must confess for a moment I'm struggling. I'm reading the answer, Mr. Hidic, and I'll trying to see if there's a link. I asked you whether for the period - I'll add those words - for the period before April 1992 you say there were any documents. And you went on to tell us something about the second half of 1992. So I must repeat it: Do you say that there were or were not any documents for the period before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it was a misunderstanding. I'm saying that until April 1992, or more specifically, the second half of 1991, there was the People's Council for Defence. I have just remembered the name of that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that in your previous answer where you referred to the second half of 1992, that that was a slip, and that you meant the second half of 1991? Is that what you're now saying?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure any more now. Either it was a slip of the tongue or it is your mistake. But I was talking about the second half of 1991 because in your question you referred to the period before April 1992, if I remember your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do remember my question correctly, Mr. Hidic, certainly. Did you conduct any examination yourself of any documentation for a period before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't personally look for it. But there was such documentation. It existed. And I got hold of it because people seemed to think that I am some sort of amateur historian, a record keeper of our times. So I got hold of the minutes of two meetings of the Council for National Defence that took place in 1991, when this body was functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, listening to your questions, I wonder whether these are really issues that were triggered by my questions. I asked specifically about how this witness received or retrieved the documents that are in the binder. I didn't ask any question about periods about other documents. If there's one or more questions, please put them to the witness, but could you please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll certainly keep it short. But I understand the principle in this context not simply to be whether -- well, the principle to be whether the issues were triggered by your questions. So it's not, in fact -- it's not what your question was related to, Your Honour, but what the answer was that came out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. But if that would be an answer that is related to a lot of subjects that have been dealt with during examination-in-chief or in cross-examination, then the mere fact that an answer is given which gives a new tiny bit of information should not open the door for a whole new line of questions which do not relate that much to the clear subject of questioning on my side. If you have one or more questions, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think probably rather than debate the principles with Your Honour, we would just have to deal with each specific matter as it came up in the course of the case. Yes, I don't think I'll attempt any more demolition of any more brick walls, Your Honour. So I'll end my questioning there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Before I'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom, I'd first like to deal with the documents tendered in relation to this witness. Madam Registrar, could you please read the list of exhibits tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that, now my recollection as well, they were tendered yesterday. There was no objection in respect of the set of documents. That's P90 containing I think it was 45 tabs of documents. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that also includes the statements of this witness. And that I think there were four, if I'm not -- Madam Registrar, would you please repeat the numbers of those four statements because -- and the dates so that it's clear what is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P86 is the witness statement dated the 3rd of November 1999. P86.1 is the translation. P87 is the witness statement dated 16 July 2000. P87.1, the translation. P88, Witness statement dated 21 May 2003. P88.1, the translation. P89, amendments to witness statement dated 30 July 2001. And P89.1 the translation. P90 is a binders of documents containing 45 tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis, is there anything you would like to raise in respect of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two other matters relating to documents and this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday you recall that the last exhibit I talked about with the defendant [sic] on direct was tab 30 in Exhibit 90, which was a document from my English translation at the time said the Bosanski Petrovac country club, but we clarified with the interpreters that that would be Bosanski Petrovac ex-patriots' club. Our language assistant has made the corrections and changed country club to ex-patriots' club, and I have that document to insert in the binders in the appropriate place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bit of a waste of paper, Mr. Hannis, because, if I'm not wrong, in the public hearing of the Brdjanin case where this same witness testified, the attention was already drawn to the fact that this was a wrong translation. So I do not see why it should be tendered in a wrong version such a long time after that. But anyhow, it's now there, the right translation. Anything further issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Second matter, Your Honour, was at the time we introduced the defendant's [sic] written statements to the ICTY, he also confirmed in his testimony that his prior testimony in Brdjanin as true, correct and accurate, and we asked the Court to consider that under Rule 92 bis (D) but we did not have copies of the transcript. Today we have copies of the transcripts from his testimony on 22 May and 26 May 2003. And we propose to tender that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Does that include the examination-in-chief or also cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That includes his entire examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Entire examination. Yes. Madam Registrar, would you please give the numbers to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript of the 22nd of May 2003 is Exhibit Number P91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will not decide on the admission of this evidence at this very moment because Rule 92 bis, even Rule 92 bis (D) has some tests in it. And since we have not read this, these transcripts, the Chamber first has to satisfy itself that it's admissible evidence, and it notes that the Defence has no objection against admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think numbering needs a bit of attention first. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the transcript of the 26th of May 2003 is Exhibit Number P92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have got two numbers for the two transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a small point, a few minutes ago Mr. Hannis's slip of the tongue referred to, "At the time we introduced the defendant's statements to the ICTY." And he meant it as the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further submissions in respect of the admission into evidence of the documents, transcripts? I take it's an oral submission now under 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nothing on that -- in that area, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to excuse the witness and ask Madam Usher to escort him out of the courtroom, but not after having thanked you, Mr. Hidic, for coming to this Tribunal and answering questions, questions from both parties, questions from the Bench. And well, we're still before the weekend. I don't know how your return is scheduled, but I hope you're soon safe home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also thank you, and I wish you a lot of success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you put on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Your Honour, a couple of points: The first is this: Although I'm informed and understand that it's not the normal practice, and indeed, it's apparent in this case it's not the normal practice, we would wish transcripts of this case and of the evidence to be available in B/C/S for Mr. Krajisnik. In a sense, the reason is obvious. Mr. Krajisnik needs to follow the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Am I well informed if I think that there are no written transcripts in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honour. Only the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are videotapes and audiotapes as well, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and audiotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your concern mainly to be that Mr. Krajisnik also has access to evidence in this Court. I don't know whether you would say that it should be necessarily be in writing or that providing Mr. Krajisnik with audiotapes and/or videotapes which he can check what the testimony is about which the other party seeks to be admitted. I don't know whether you have given that some thought, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I haven't, Your Honour, except in the last 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But on the other hand, the last 30 seconds is really -- I don't claim it's enough for my brain to process all possibilities, but it is enough for me to have some fairly solid thoughts which are these: That audiotapes and videotapes don't come anywhere near providing the equivalent of transcripts because it's absolutely familiar to all of us that a person can read a transcript far, far faster than the actual time taken on an audiotape or a videotape, by a factor of many. So it doesn't provide the equivalent. Therefore, that wouldn't do the essential task which is that it is absolutely vital that as this case progresses and the evidence piles up, that Mr. Krajisnik is -- and after all at some point we will get to the presentation of Mr. Krajisnik's defence, his case, that Mr. Krajisnik is able to read the evidence that has been given against him, well, for practical purposes whenever he wants. And it simply won't be manageable for him to do it by audiotape and videotape. I'm sure if anybody just pictures that for a few seconds, one can see how impossible that will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say it's a very -- it's a matter of principle. It's a fundamental issue you're raising here. It also has great practical implications. So let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber finds that it would be appropriate to raise this matter in writing, because it's a fundamental issue, so that we can see and hear the response of the Prosecution. At the same time, I think just raising the matter should make the Prosecution start thinking, at least for 30 seconds, on the issue in respect of perhaps limiting to the necessary the evidence presented which exists at this moment on paper only in one of the official languages of the Tribunal, but the matter is important enough to submitted to the Chamber in writing so that it can read the response and perhaps you give the sources and the case law of the Tribunal so that we are in a better position to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will add that to our "to do" list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will see what comes out of this "to do" list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think it's the last thing immediately, is that we have provided for the Tribunal a small batch of correspondence. It actually needs additions of two items. It may be Mr. Harmon's going to deal with both those additional items.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have for purposes, Mr. Stewart, of completeness of the package that you presented to me, I've given you already an extra set of copies of one correspondence, and during the -- before Court started, I went and got another complete set of copies of correspondence. So they are available here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there are two additional letters. It was an initial exchange of correspondence between myself and Mr. Harmon, one letter from me to him and another letter from him to me. I've got -- I think the practical position, I've got Mr. Harmon's letter to me of the 23rd, and that's going to come to Your Honours from the -- from Mr. Harmon. And then my letter to him same day, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I gave you all my copies --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, you did. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- of my response. And here's a copy for the Court of your letter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see. In that case, Ms. Philpott, if we deluge you with this stuff. These are Mr. Harmon's letter to me, and Mr. Harmon has provided my letter to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you want us to read this, and may I ask you whether we need to deal with the matter before today 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Only this, Your Honour: The matter, in fact, goes back to the beginning of the trial. But it has taken a little time to sort out and get to this stage. I'm just reluctant to leave it very much longer. But Your Honour I can't say that it's absolutely essential that it gets dealt with today. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we'll do, then. I had in mind that we would have a break of half an hour in order to further discuss among the Judges the item that was still on the agenda. That we'll now take 40 minutes -- well, let's say three-quarters of an hour. We'll then adjourn until 10 minutes past 1.00. And would have, then, some time to briefly discuss or to inform you about the position of the Chamber in respect of the other issues on the agenda. But before deciding so, I'll just consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 1.00. But the fact that we are reading the material just provided to us doesn't mean that the Chamber already agrees that it should be dealt with at such short notice. So we'll read it, and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. It's there to see where we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We then stand adjourned until 10 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Stewart, that the Defence had sufficient opportunity to discuss with Mr. Krajisnik the -- I would say the ongoing discussions between the parties and the...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please use your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. He knows in bear outline, Your Honour. We -- in fact, the issue has been under discussion for some time between him and us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's then fine. What we'll discuss or speak about on the next perhaps 15 to 20 minutes is an issue that would be usually raised during a Status Conference but -- well, whether we call it a Status Conference or part of this trial is not of major importance, I would say, but it's practical matters rather than anything else. First of all, before we start discussing any scheduling, the parties are informed that the Judges have read the correspondence about certain press publications and at this moment the Chamber finds that it's sufficient to establish that the Chamber is now fully informed about the ongoing discussions. We'll leave it to that at this moment. Then I'd like to move to the subject of the scheduling of the trial for the next month, up till the summer break. The parties have discussed and even agreed upon getting some additional time from the Chamber in order to have further meetings and to see whether what exactly are the points that are most in dispute and where presentation of evidence would not be really necessary because matters might not be in dispute. The Chamber, first of all, has tried to analyse a bit what happened over the last couple of weeks. And our findings are that the evidence presented until now, as far as the Prosecution was concerned, took approximately 17, 18 per cent less time than it was estimated. The Defence cross-examining these witnesses stayed also approximately within the -- I would say the guideline or at least the -- 60 per cent of the time taken in chief, so that is not only 17 per cent gained from -- in time -- Prosecution time but also in Defence time. On the other hand, the 92 bis cross-examination takes a bit more time than the Chamber calculated in the beginning. But overall the parties are staying within the limits we calculated and the estimates they have given to the Chamber. That is certainly an encouraging circumstance for further accommodating the parties in what they're asking for. The Chamber therefore is inclined to give some additional time to the parties mainly for two reasons. I think they are combined reasons. One of them is to give the Defence a better opportunity to get on the top of the case, as it's often expressed, which would also include, of course, discussions with Mr. Krajisnik himself and -- well, to be better prepared than they feel they are now. At the same time this time could be used to define those issues that are not in dispute and to see whether the parties could agree on a presentation of evidence, avoiding the presentation -- unnecessary presentation of evidence. They have given the Chamber an insight in a kind of a programme of negotiations on that. Of course, the Chamber will not interfere with that, but at least the programme makes sure that the parties are serious in their efforts to achieve such a thing. The parties have asked for nine additional weeks. As I indicated before, I did not expect the Chamber would agree with nine weeks. I can confirm now that the Chamber will not agree with nine weeks. During these discussions, it also came up that time is one thing but subsequent periods of time sometimes is even of similar importance, and therefore the Chamber has tried to see how time could be granted and at the same time how the Chamber could still keep some grip on the trial. That means that the Chamber would like to -- if it grants time, that the Chamber would like to receive reports during the period in which this time is granted on any progress made as far as the effects on the trial is concerned, because the -- an expeditious trial is, of course, one thing the accused is entitled to and one of the things that is of -- certainly of concern for the Chamber. Now I have to ask the parties to take their pens and on the calendar for proposed adjournment period, we examine that week 1, starting on the 3rd of May, week 9 in this schedule starting on the 28th of June. I will refer to those numbers when I give the parties two possible solutions, two alternatives the Chamber at this moment is about to consider, and the Chamber would like to hear the preference of the parties for one of them. Let me first start with alternative 1. Alternative 1 would be that the break already scheduled, of course, we are not sitting; and then in week 1 we would not sit; in week 2, we would not sit; in weeks 3, 4, and 5, we would sit; week 6, we would not sit; weeks 7, 8, and 9 we would sit; but - that's beyond the proposed calendar - week 10 we would not sit; and then we would sit until the summer break. I can imagine the advantage of this schedule would be that there are three weeks to start with altogether in which we would not sit; that is, the break already scheduled in week 1 and week 2. Then the alternative schedule, which grants a bit more of time but in a different way -- a little bit -- yes, a little bit more time but in a different way, would be the following: After the break already scheduled, in week 1 we would not sit; week 2 we would sit but not necessarily on from Monday. We could start on Wednesday or -- or Thursday. In week 3, we would also sit; in week 4, we would compensate for the few days of week 2, where we were not sitting, so if we would start on Wednesday in week 2, we would then sit on Monday and Tuesday in week 4, unless in week 2, part of it, and week 3 we would hear evidence which would have been anymore to compensate in the beginning of week 4... calculated as normal for two whole weeks, so there's nothing any more to compensate in the beginning of week 4. So there's some flexibility about week 2 and 3. We could start a bit later. If we are really very efficient in hearing evidence, it might be that we will need no compensation any more in week 4 but, otherwise, we would sit for one or two days in week 4 as well. Then the rest of the week 4, of course, we would not sit; week 5, we would not sit; week 6, we would sit; the same for week 7, we would sit; and would then not sit during week 8 and week 9 of the schedule; and then starting on the 5th of July, we would sit until the summer break. As I said before, these two schedules, we'd start with one of them but on the basis of the reports we'll see whether we could finalise them as we now provisionally have scheduled. The parties are invited in their reporting, especially in the early reporting, not to deal exclusively with the easy parts but also with the more problematic parts. If, for example, I look at expert witnesses in the beginning who are scheduled for 92 bis and are scheduled for cross-examination for perhaps one hour, then of course five or six expert witnesses would save only relative time. But let's not discuss the details. But the Chamber would like to be informed about the progress made, to receive reports on that or to meet in that respect, and we'll certainly, then, also have a look on whether more problematic issues also result in -- in identifying issues not in dispute. So it's -- we'd make a start. And the Chamber is quite confident that the parties will try to do their utmost best to achieve the aims. At the same time, I have to emphasise that on from September the Chamber expects that we would sit five days a week and apart from one week off - and we still have to decide which one - but one week off in autumn that we'd still at the regular basis. I also inform you that, just in order to better be able to calculate what is advantageous and what is not, that Monday, the 31st of May we would not sit anyhow because it's a UN holiday. In the one schedule we would sit that week; that means that we would not sit for five days but only four days that week. In the other schedule, that week, which is week 5, we would not sit; so that would include that UN holiday. This is what the Chamber would like to bring to your attention at this moment and ask whether the parties could express any preference for one of these alternative solutions: The one resulting in a little bit more time but not three weeks in the beginning; the other one a little bit less time but three weeks in the beginning, and the last week not sitting, being week 10, which was beyond the original schedule. Whom of the parties could I...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the request was a Defence request, so I would defer to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- hearing them first. The Prosecution's response to their request was in -- so the record is perfectly clear, we were more than willing to sit and engage the Defence in identifying areas in which we could perhaps compress the presentation of evidence as well as assist the Defence in other areas. But so the record is clear, this was not our request, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence position is very plain. Neither of these proposals is remotely adequate. They are both hopelessly inadequate, and we are not prepared to indicate any preference or any election between them. Now that -- we're grateful to the Tribunal for making the position clear, and it is important that the matter is now brought into open court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- after discussions, and we appreciate that. It is quite plain that we, the Defence, have failed sufficiently to explain and bring to the understanding of the Tribunal the state of this case and the pressures and difficulties under which the Defence is operating and the serious gap that still exists between any normal state of preparation which Mr. Krajisnik is entitled to expect in relation to such serious charges, and where we are or where we can prospectively be. It's probably, therefore, not particularly valuable or sensible for me to say more this afternoon because we have not, as Your Honour acknowledged in the meeting we had yesterday evening, we have not made full submissions in relation to this matter. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We wrote a fairly long letter. Consequently, the right which Your Honour recognised all of us had in our meeting yesterday evening, which is to formally bring the matter before the Court by way of a motion for a more substantial adjournment is a right which we will exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so that is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, just complete in one sentence, that I did indicated this morning that I would therefore have in those circumstances a more qualified motion today or application to at least see us over the interim period while that matter is ventilated, while the matter is fully decided, so that at least we do have some practical course. And I would welcome the opportunity of doing that. While I'm on my feet, may I also say, because I indicated yesterday, that so far as the proposal from September onwards is concerned, which is completely different issue, we do wish express here - and would wish to ventilate this on a future occasion - the enormous discrepancy between what the Defence team were led to believe was the likely timetable when we were brought into this case on the basis of specific information coming from this institution. It is not a question, we believe, of anybody misleading us in relation to that information; it is a question of this institution, it not being appropriate for this institution as a whole, despite the demands and the pressures, to create such an enormous gap between what counsel are told is going to be involved in a case when they're brought into it and what actually happens. I so say no more about that because it's important that I should have chapter and verse, I should have that information, I should be able to explain to the Tribunal exactly what the position was and exactly what the basis was on which the case was presented to us and on which we came into it, because it's not fair to expect the Tribunal to make any final judgement on that without having that information, without feeling -- about having submissions. It's also a very delicate area because there is a sentence in which it ultimately involves potentially some conflict between the position of counsel and their own client, because some balance -- after all, nobody sits seven days a week on these cases, some balance has to be achieved. I do recognise that. But on the other hand, nobody is without some legitimate interest in this matter. So I simply put that on the record and reserve my position, because it is a matter on which we are fully entitled to make submissions. But it's obviously also a matter that we should very importantly discuss with our -- our client. But the fundamental aim here is to have a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik and to have him have the opportunity of presenting his case fairly but in a way, of course, that is consistent with all the other requirements of justice and is, to an appropriate extent, consistent with fairness to all involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, Mr. Stewart, your position. Then the parties have also invited the Chamber to make clear what's going to happen during the next few weeks, because the Prosecution needs to further prepare the presentation of its evidence. The Chamber was willing to -- either to decide on alternative 1 or alternative 2, where the Defence indicates that it will file a motion for further time, I think it would be improper for the Chamber to now decide on alternative 1 or 2 and only to decide on short term what's going to happen, awaiting a submission by the Defence. I could indicate that as matters stand now -- stand now the Chamber could be expected, then, to decide that we would not sit in week 1, so that would mean that we would not sit for the next two weeks, and that the Prosecution should prepare for resuming on Monday, the 10th of May, which is the second week in the schedule, and we would then, of course, by then have to consider the motion filed, then, by the Defence; we would then consider the response given by the Prosecution in that respect; and we would then give a decision on whether any additional time, apart from the one week given now, would be granted. So therefore, the Chamber will -- one thing is for sure: Whether we are in alternative 1 or in alternative 2 or in a position where the Chamber has not decided because it expects a submission by the Defence asking for more time, we'll not sit anyhow in the week of the 3rd of May. As far as the week of Monday, the 10th of May is concerned, we would not sit under alternative 1, we would at least, the second half of the week, sit under alternative 2, and we would resume on Monday, the 10th of May if we have to decide on a motion for further time to be granted. If the parties are determined, even without consulting -- further consultation of clients, that's the position as taken now, that alternative 1 and alternative 2 are both unacceptable and no preference could be expressed, then I will give a decision -- the Chamber will give a decision now that would -- could be expected to be not to sit on the week of the 3rd of May and then to restart on the 10th of May and see what happens. If, however, the Defence would further -- would like further to consult with Mr. Krajisnik and tell us, well, within -- say, within the next hour, hour and a half, then we could give a decision later today, which would be any -- I would say any of the three options. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm not offering a suggestion as to an alternative, given this is not precipitated by our request; this is a Defence request. I've heard the Defence, and therefore I don't think it's my position to -- to at this point in time express a preference. I've heard what the Defence has to say. I thank you very much for your consideration, Mr. President, Your Honours, of the request that has been made and taking the time to listen to us, and I will await further decision from the Defence and then take my lead, in terms of preparing the case and preparing the witnesses to show up at the next scheduled trial session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart, does the Defence want some additional time to consider the situation, or do you say, "Well, no, it's clear to us."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't -- we don't need additional time to consider the situation, nor to consult Mr. Krajisnik. I merely ask for the opportunity to make the submissions, which I've indicated I wish to make, as to the short term, in the light of the fact that we proposed to file a motion for a more substantial adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The position is this, Your Honour: As far as next week is concerned - not week 1 on the schedule but the week's break - I -- I have arranged to stay in The Hague until Tuesday night. My co-counsel and our case manager, I believe, are going to be in The Hague the whole week. I can tell Your Honour that I shall not be in a position to work on this case from Wednesday morning through to Sunday evening. I'm perfectly happy to explain the reasons. They are essentially a combination of professional and personal. They are in fact largely personal, as it happens, over that period. I make no bones about that. The -- and I -- my proposal is and was to come back to The Hague on Sunday night. So it's -- it's not really a complete working week. In the situation in which we are, such time as is available over that very short period, the substantial amount of it will have to be devoted to preparing this motion, which in a sense is sort of time wasted but -- but anyway, it's -- it has to be done, and in fact the combination of that and the immediate tidying up after a couple of weeks of sitting is -- is going to take that period, and it will, for practical purposes, probably take the week for the rest of my team -- assuming they take absolutely no time off, a position which actually I would resist and discourage them from adopting because they need it and are entitled to it. That's why I didn't include next week as a numbered week in the schedule, because I think it's unfair and unrealistic for us to count that as a live working week anyway. So I started off at week 1. Your Honour knows - and I have made it clear - that I do urgently need to go to Bosnia. I was intending to go during the break. That was the plan. But I couldn't. Ms. Loukas and my case manager went; I simply did not have the time to go with them. I have been once for an extremely short time with my case manager. It's essential for me to go largely to consult with and give direction and to spend time with our team of investigators out there, but also because I do actually need to see one or two things out there anyway for myself. And before the case gets very far along the line, I need to do that. It should have really happened before, but needs must and it wasn't possible. It won't make sense for me to go immediately after I get back on Sunday night, to go straight off on Monday, because there will be preparation to be done here to ensure that everything is in hand and in shape for the period when I am away. It will also be necessary to make preparation for that visit. I should also add, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just interrupt you. You know that we are limited in time until quarter to 2.00. Part of what you said is already in your letter, the function of the necessity of going to Bosnia. Could you speed up and see whether we can -- I mean, the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Your Honour, I hadn't noticed the time, as it happens. But the fact that it's in my letter is not really a total answer, Your Honour. I have to take Ms. Cmeric with me as well to Bosnia. For practical purposes. I have to do that. There's no other way of doing that. I don't speak the language myself and taking somebody else will not enable me to establish rapport and to hold those meetings and she knows about the case, so she has to come. Ms. Loukas will therefore be on her own here. If we go for one week, which is actually a realistic estimate -- we will be back sometime in the middle of week 2. If our trip is to be valuable, we're going to have things to do in the light of that as well. It is simply not realistic, we suggest, for us then to be preparing for week 3, another week of evidence. Ms. Loukas will be here on her own without our case manager for much of that period. There are all sorts of other things to be done. So the short-term proposal is this, Your Honour: We also -- another reason why we can't go to Bosnia until the middle of week 1 is because we have to have this motion dealt with. We would apprehend that the Prosecution's time for responding to the motion wouldn't take very long because the Prosecution have adopted a -- I may say, a helpful relatively neutral position, so I don't suppose they would have very much to say. What we're proposing Your Honour, is that we file that motion, but that motion comes on for hearing and submissions very early in that week, and we are entirely in the Tribunal's hands as to when that might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that week would then be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's week 1. In week 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's the week of Monday, the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Monday, the 3rd. That we should -- that that motion should be heard, just that motion, that that should be dealt with as early as the Tribunal saw fit in that week. As soon as that motion has been dealt with, or within a day or so anyway, Ms. Cmeric and I would be able to get off to Bosnia. We would be back sometime in week 2. We would therefore ask for week 3 not sitting because it is excessively burdensome and difficult for us to then been in a position to deal with week 3 in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to write it down. Mr. Stewart, you are asking to hear in week 1 your motion, in week -- in the beginning of week 1 and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the beginning of week 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then no further sittings that week. And then in week 2 you would like not to sit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And week 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And week 3 as well, not to sit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because we won't even be back -- Ms. Cmeric and I won't even be back from Bosnia until sometime well into week 2. And it will incidentally -- it is now quarter to 2.00, Your Honour, but it's not as if nothing can be done. We do have -- Your Honour knows we do have interns working on -- continuing to work on sorting all the material. Ms. Loukas will be here. There will be all sorts of things she can do. But for Ms. Loukas to then prepare on her own without the case manager to be ready to deal with week 3 evidence would simply be oppressive, and we won't be in a position to do that and make productive use of this important trip to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... spent time with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've stressed several times the importance of the trip to Bosnia. Of course, especially in alternative 1, that would give a better opportunity to fulfil that job. And what flexibility there could then be in weeks 3, 4, and 5 is a different matter. If that would be something that you would like to further discuss, I'm willing to do that. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Alternative 1, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, as such -- let me just consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As such, hearing a motion on the 3rd of May, if we would have received by then also the response of the -- of the Prosecution is a possibility the Chamber would not deny. But that does not mean that you would have an opportunity then to go to Bosnia, because we'll then have to decide on your motion. And as I indicated before, the Chamber was determined that if option 1 -- alternative 1 or alternative 2 would not be there, that we would continue on the 10th of May. We're also willing to wait until the 10th of May to hear your motion. Meanwhile continuing, and then see whatever schedule after we have continued, at least during that first week, giving the Prosecution the opportunity to examine the witnesses presented that week, what would be the outcome of that. If you want us to hear a motion on the 3rd of May, you prevent yourself from going to Bosnia any earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour is forcing me to elect between these two alternatives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- without my having been given the opportunity of making proper submissions on the matter. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You can make whatever submissions you want, but it seems to be more or less included in your claim for making submissions that you would then have an opportunity to go to Bosnia, which is, well, preluding more or less on what our decision would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to go to Bosnia. It's an essential requirement of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm doing at the moment, Your Honour, is presenting to Your Honour as fairly as we possibly can what are essential requirements to provide a proper defence for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have already given up on the trip to Bosnia in order to meet the -- the relentless timetable imposed on us by this Tribunal before Easter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honour knows how -- how very reluctant we were to do that and how very cooperative we were in order to get this trial started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, in alternative 1 -- in alternative 1 you would have -- we would not sit in week 1, we would not sit in week 2, and as I indicated, we could see how flexible we could be for the beginning of week 3. There's another possibility: That you file the motion and you write down everything you would like to say, that we see what the response of the Prosecution is, and that we would then give a decision on the basis of the written submissions. That's another possibility that would not make it necessary to be here on Monday, the 3rd of May. What I'm saying is that if you do not express any preference, we'll wait until we've received your motion, until we have received your submissions, and we would then decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem with either of the preferences is week 3 -- and in effect, all I am asking from the Tribunal today is for you to add to the short-term position week 3, because it is clear from what I'm saying that it is that that is the problem, because it is -- it is the insistence by the Tribunal that we will sit in week 3 which is creating the problem. It's a single week in this whole exercise over a trial estimated to last more than two years. This is creating the problem, because it does not give Ms. Cmeric and I the opportunity to go to Bosnia and to do the proper work in Bosnia and be back and for everybody to be ready for week 3. It is one week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: If we would not sit in week 3, would you be willing to give up one of the later weeks we would not sit? So week 10 in alternative 1 or week 8 or week 9 in alternative 2? Since you're stressing so much week 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not accept -- I think there's a logical flaw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not fair -- with respect, it's not fair the way Your Honour puts the question, because we have already indicated that we do not regard in the interests of a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik either alternative as acceptable. So for Your Honour to ask me, once again, to trade off week 3 for some implicit election for one of these two proposals, which Your Honour knows we don't accept, is with respect not a fair way of approaching the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's fair or not, I asked you a question. I received an answer to that question. We'll now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Madam Registrar already received the translation of a document, but that's not very urgent at this moment, so we'll deal with that after the break. The Chamber will finally decide this afternoon when we'll resume the trial, and for the time being the parties should be prepared to appear on the 10th of May -- Monday, the 10th of May. And during the next hour the Chamber will -- if there's anything else the parties would like to discuss with the Chamber, the Presiding Judge is available and we'll then further consider the matter and we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can make just two brief observations, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, the Defence had desperately wanted this matter to be resolved before this break. And may we remind Your Honour that our letter went astray for a week which has created enormous difficulty, and we have been urging that this matter be dealt with. And the second point is the suggestion that the whole matter might be dealt with by submissions in writing. It is enormously burdensome to have to cover such an issue entirely in writing, and it is not, we suggest, appropriate either. It is absolutely appropriate that this matter of what is required in order to enable Mr. Krajisnik to have a fair trial should be openly discussed in court and not dealt with simply in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to respond to that, whether the letter went astray for one week or whether the Chamber urged the parties to see what additional information could be provided in order to make it easier for the Chamber to decide on the issues raised in that letter. I'm not going to respond on that. The Chamber will give a decision this afternoon, and during the next hour if there would be anything additional to be brought to the attention of the Chamber, the Chamber is willing to receive that. We'll adjourn, as far as it stands now, until 10th of May.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.56 p.m.,
